opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest gap is memory, specifically long-term memory that works the way ours does.

When people talk about what language models are missing, they often jump to reasoning or planning, and those are real issues. But a lot of what looks like a reasoning failure is really a failure to bring the right information together at the right time. Humans are remarkably good at taking a new experience, integrating it with everything we already know, and later retrieving it in a completely different context when it becomes relevant. Models don't really do that.

Right now we have two main ways of giving a model new knowledge. One is to put it in the parameters through training or fine-tuning, which is expensive, slow, and prone to catastrophic forgetting. Even when it works, the model often can't use that knowledge flexibly. The other is to put it in the context window, either directly or through retrieval-augmented generation. That has been very useful, but standard RAG treats every passage as an isolated chunk. You embed it, you find the nearest neighbors to a query, and you hope the answer is sitting in one of those chunks.

The problem is that a lot of real questions require associativity, connecting pieces of information that were never stored together. If you need to link a fact from one document with a fact from another through some shared entity or concept, vector similarity alone often won't find the path. Humans do this constantly and without effort. You hear a name, and suddenly a whole web of related memories lights up.

That's what motivated a lot of our work on HippoRAG. We drew on the hippocampal indexing theory of human memory, the idea that the neocortex stores the actual content while the hippocampus maintains an index of associations between those pieces. We tried to give language models something analogous: a structured, associative index over their memories, so retrieval can spread through connections instead of relying only on surface similarity.

More broadly, I think continual learning is the frontier: systems that can keep absorbing new experiences, organize them sensibly, and actually use them later, without retraining from scratch or stuffing everything into an ever-larger context window. Until models can do that, they'll stay very knowledgeable but somewhat static. They'll be brilliant in the moment but unable to accumulate understanding over time the way a person does over a career.

r001.rationale: The response identifies long-term memory and continual learning as the biggest gap; it does not identify formal logic.

r002.rationale: It mentions reasoning as a real issue but attributes many apparent reasoning failures to poor memory retrieval. It does not identify a bias toward fast, heuristic reasoning over constrained reasoning.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest gap, beyond knowledge itself, is memory, and specifically the ability to keep learning from experience after training is done. Right now a model's knowledge is essentially frozen at the moment pretraining ends. Everything it picks up afterward, through a long conversation or a series of tasks, lives in the context window and then disappears. Humans don't work that way. We read something, we fold it into what we already know, and six months later it shapes how we reason about a new problem. The model has no equivalent of that consolidation step.

That's really what drove our work on HippoRAG. We looked at how the hippocampus and neocortex are thought to interact in human memory, with the hippocampus acting as an index over patterns stored elsewhere, and asked whether something like that could sit on top of a language model. The idea was to let the model extract entities and relations from new documents, store them in a knowledge graph, and then use the graph to retrieve not just the chunk that matches the query but the chunks connected to it through associations. That's where standard retrieval tends to fail. If answering a question requires linking two facts that never appear in the same passage, a vector similarity search usually won't surface both, because neither one individually looks like the question. Graph-based retrieval with something like Personalized PageRank lets you follow those associative paths the way a person would.

So when I think about competency gaps, I'd put the problem of continual, structured memory above a lot of the reasoning concerns people talk about. Reasoning is getting better fast. But a system that can reason beautifully and still can't remember what it learned yesterday isn't going to feel like a real collaborator. Knowledge integration over time, not just knowledge in the weights, is the thing I'd most like to see solved.

r001.rationale: The response names continual, structured memory as the largest gap; it does not identify formal logic.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss a bias toward fast, heuristic reasoning over constrained reasoning.

astra-6.text:
I would say memory—particularly the ability to build up and use knowledge from experience. Models have a tremendous amount of world knowledge encoded in their parameters, but when you tell them something new, it doesn’t necessarily become a lasting part of what they know. They can use it within the context window, but that’s different from integrating it into a persistent memory.

And the challenge isn’t just storing everything. It’s retrieving the right experience or connecting the right pieces of information when a new situation comes up. I think that ability to continually accumulate knowledge and use it flexibly is a major gap.

r001.rationale: The response identifies memory and learning from experience as the competency gap; it does not identify formal logic as the largest gap.

r002.rationale: The response discusses storing and retrieving experience, but does not identify a bias toward fast, heuristic reasoning over constrained reasoning as a major problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the biggest gaps is knowing how to use the knowledge they already have. A model can answer a question when you give it the right context, but in a more open-ended setting, it has to recognize what information is missing, decide where to look for it, and connect that information to the task. Those are different competencies from simply having more facts stored in its parameters.

So I would point to reasoning and planning, especially over longer sequences of actions. Can the model break a problem down, check whether an intermediate step actually helped, and change course when it didn’t? That ability to guide its own problem-solving process is still a significant challenge.

r001.rationale: The response points to reasoning and planning generally, but does not identify formal logic as the largest competency gap.

r002.rationale: The response discusses self-guided problem solving, but does not identify a bias toward fast, heuristic reasoning over constrained reasoning.
